Title: Fight Oligarchy
Author: Bernie Sanders
My Review:
Very high level and low on substance

This book provides a very high level overview of struggles for workers rights and general liberty in the United States and across the world. Anyone who is a student of history is not going to find any new information there.

Additionally, this book provides a section on Bernie's own recommendations on what changes need to be instituted. However, it fails to provide explanations or mechanisms on the sustainability of those recommendations, leaving the reader concerned for how well thought out those positions are. I am personally saddened by this because while I may agree with some of his points, his failure to explain them adequately undermines them and leaves the reader (myself) worried that they are not well thought through.

This book additionally provides a high level overview of some of the campaign work that Bernie has been doing, which really isn't particularly interesting or valuable for trying to convince people of his position.

In short, I may agree with a lot of what you believe, but as an engineer, having read this book leaves me upset that you present your life's work as not well thought through. It felt like I was reading an extended collage of brief campaign clips. But maybe I was not a part of the intended audience for this book.

Title: The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America
Author: Richard Rothstein
My Review:
This will likely be my go to book for book recommendations for the foreseeable future.

This book reviews the history of de jure (state sanctioned) segregation in the USA (civil war through today). Over 194 pages, Richard Rothstein covers this history of de jure segregation, its systemic and multi-generational impact, the progress made against it, and how there is still much to be done to heal this injustice - he does so with a preponderance of historical examples (there are 71 pages of notes and bibliography). This history includes other prominent themes such as the delayed full execution of civil-rights laws (in some instances taking decades to be full upheld / executed) and repeated attempts to skirt them by government officials in all branches.

The epilogue does a very nice job of succinctly summarizing the classes of this de jure segregation and how it has impacted people of color: https://erenow.com/modern/color-of-law-forgotten-history/14.php

At the end, Rothstein spends an additional 23 pages on recommended paths forward.

I wish that I had had this book (and read it) during the time of my own high school / college education. The completeness of Rothstein's writing on the topic has substantially impacted my understanding of US history - at time reinforcing and at times upending. It has greatly augmented my understanding of US history for the better.

Richard Rothstein - thank you for writing this book.
